guides.title: Buddhist temples, monasteries and networks
guides.description: From early Indian stupas to pilgrimage, scholarship and temple patronage across Asia.
guides.intro: Buddhism arose in South Asia in the first millennium BCE. Over many centuries, worshippers, translators and rulers created distinct religious landscapes across Asia. A stupa at Sanchi, a manuscript from Dunhuang and the Great Buddha at Nara show different ways people built communities around Buddhist practice.
guides.scope: Selected institutions from South Asia to Sri Lanka, Tibet, eastern Asia and Southeast Asia. Site ages identify particular monuments or phases of use. They often postdate the earliest local Buddhist communities.

map.scope: Approximate places on modern terrain, from South Asia to Indian Ocean and Silk Roads institutions, Tibet and Japan. The markers locate examples discussed in the guide.

sections.heading: The Buddha and the places of pilgrimage

paragraphs.text: Buddhist traditions connect Siddhartha Gautama’s awakening to Bodh Gaya and his birth to Lumbini. His exact lifetime is debated, but Buddhism’s origins lie several centuries before the Common Era. The Aśokan pillar at Lumbini records a royal visit in the third century BCE, placing a pilgrimage tradition in the historical record centuries after the Buddha’s life.

Teachings about suffering, ethical conduct and paths to liberation traveled through oral instruction, texts and communities of practice. Stupas could hold relics or commemorate a person or event. Walking clockwise around a stupa made worship a physical practice. Sanchi’s original Mauryan monument was enlarged, and its gates and sculpture belong to later periods of investment.

Buddhist communities depended on relations between people who left household life and people who provided food, property, money or labor. Commissioning an image or monument and giving to a community were ways of seeking religious merit. At Indian sites, inscriptions preserve gifts from laypeople and from monks and nuns. The named sponsors of images make the economic and devotional roles of women visible.

In Sri Lanka, Anuradhapura combined royal patronage with longstanding monastic communities. The sacred Bodhi tree is revered as a descendant of the tree at Bodh Gaya. The tradition linking those trees made a South Asian place of awakening present in the ritual and political life of another island capital.

A ninth-century copperplate from Nalanda records King Devapāla’s grant of five villages at the request of Bālaputradeva, a ruler based in Sumatra. The grant supported the monks, the monastery’s upkeep and the copying of texts. It ties an Indian monastery to patrons across the Bay of Bengal and to the agricultural resources that sustained scholarship on the ground.

At Nalanda, monks lived and studied in a network of brick monasteries and shrines. The seventh-century Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang studied there. His travels and writing connect a specific institution with the movement of teachers, books and pilgrims across linguistic and political frontiers.

Dunhuang’s caves preserve painted ritual settings and manuscripts from successive regimes at a Silk Roads oasis. A printed Diamond Sutra dated 868 names Wang Jie in its colophon and records that he had it made for distribution on behalf of his parents. This surviving book shows how copying and circulating a scripture could express family devotion and make religious merit visible.

Longmen’s patrons cut individual niches and enormous sculptures into cliffs near Luoyang. At Nara, Emperor Shōmu’s government supported Tōdai-ji and provincial temples and nunneries. Such projects brought together resources, ritual specialists and artisans to make Buddhism visible within political life.

Patronage could be withdrawn. Tang emperor Wuzong’s edict of 845 ordered the suppression of Buddhist institutions. Its language shows rulers treating the wealth, buildings and personnel of monasteries as political and economic issues. The edict records one government’s position in a particular crisis.

Buddhist teachers, texts and images also traveled through Indian Ocean and Southeast Asian ports. Theravāda lineages became influential in Sri Lanka and mainland Southeast Asia, while institutions shaped by Mahāyāna and esoteric teachings developed in other places. Their histories intersected with Hindu courts and local traditions. These broad designations cover many different communities and ritual practices.

Borobudur’s terraces guide visitors past reliefs and stupas. Bagan’s monuments fill a capital’s surrounding landscape. At Angkor Wat, a temple built for Vishnu later housed Buddhist worship. In Tibet, institutions such as the Potala linked particular Buddhist lineages to government. These sites show how communities made different uses of architecture and political sponsorship over time.
The date of a monument, dedication or rebuilding provides a specific anchor for each place. Early traditions and later layers of use can belong to the same site.

guides.title: Confucian temples, learning and government
guides.description: From Confucius and Mencius to academies, examinations and ritual across East Asia.
guides.intro: Confucian traditions began in first-millennium BCE China with teachings about moral formation, family relationships, ritual and public responsibility. Later courts and communities built temples to teachers, academies for study and systems for selecting officials. These institutions developed differently in China, Korea, Vietnam and Japan.
guides.scope: Selected people, texts and institutions in East Asia across three periods of change, from classical teachings to imperial academies and later regional adaptations.

map.scope: Approximate sites on modern terrain, including dedicated temples, state schools, local academies and a royal ancestral shrine.

points.label: Confucius Temple and Kong family sites, Qufu
points.date: Temple tradition from 478 BCE
points.description: The temple, Kong lineage cemetery and residence preserve distinct institutions that grew around commemoration of Confucius and his descendants.

points.label: Mencius Temple, Zoucheng
points.date: Eleventh-century foundation. Present location from 1122 CE.
points.description: A temple tradition that began near the attributed grave of Mencius moved to this site in the Northern Song. Local custodians conducted ceremonies in his honor.

points.label: White Deer Grotto Academy, Lushan
points.date: Established in 940 CE. Revived under Zhu Xi in the late twelfth century.
points.description: An academy on Mount Lu became an important center for Neo-Confucian learning in a landscape with prominent Buddhist and Daoist sites.

points.label: Temple of Literature, Hanoi
points.date: Temple founded 1070. Academy dates to 1076.
points.description: A Vietnamese royal temple to Confucius became associated with education and official examinations. The surviving stone steles record examination graduates.

points.label: Confucius Temple and Imperial College, Beijing
points.date: Confucius Temple built in 1302 CE. Adjacent college also founded under the Yuan.
points.description: An imperial temple and national school occupy adjoining precincts. Honor for teachers and canon went alongside official study and commemoration of examination success.

points.label: Seonggyungwan, Seoul
points.date: Joseon academy established 1398
points.description: The principal state academy provided classical education in the capital. The Munmyo shrine formed part of its ritual setting.

points.date: Late fourteenth-century foundation. Rebuilt in the early seventeenth century.
points.description: Rituals for the royal ancestors connected offerings, music and dance to the expression of dynastic legitimacy.

points.label: Sosuseowon Academy, Yeongju
points.date: Established in the 1540s
points.description: A pioneering Korean seowon brought study and commemoration of learned figures together in a locally supported academy.

points.description: A Confucian temple and school associated with the Hayashi family became a center of Tokugawa education.

sections.heading: Teaching and ritual in early China

paragraphs.text: Confucius, traditionally dated 551–479 BCE, taught in a period of competing states. The Analects gathers sayings and exchanges handed down by followers. It asks how a person learns to act with humanity and how ritual, including ways of honoring parents and ancestors, can shape character. Good government depends on what leaders do and how others learn from their example.

Later thinkers developed competing answers. Mencius discussed how people cultivate moral capacities and insisted that rulers must attend to the conditions in which people live. The Qufu precinct links the teacher’s temple to a cemetery and the residence of the Kong lineage. The later temple to Mencius at Zoucheng commemorates another early thinker through a local and publicly sponsored ritual history.

sections.heading: Temples, schools and access to office

paragraphs.text: At Beijing’s Confucius Temple and Imperial College, ritual recognition of learned predecessors and education for government stood side by side. In later imperial China, exams tested mastery of classical writing and interpretation. They became a major route into official service and helped circulate a common curriculum. Preparation took money and time, and many trained candidates never became officials.

Women were excluded from regular examination access, although women studied, wrote and taught in household and other settings. Ban Zhao’s Han-period admonitions promoted gendered duties while also making a case for educating girls. Reading her work beside later examination records shows how learning could be valued while official opportunities remained sharply unequal.

sections.heading: Reworking the classics in Buddhist and Daoist settings

paragraphs.text: Song thinkers reread earlier works in intellectual worlds also shaped by Buddhist and Daoist institutions. Zhu Xi brought the Analects, Mencius, Great Learning and Doctrine of the Mean together as the Four Books, emphasizing disciplined study and investigation. At Mount Lu he revived White Deer Grotto Academy. Buddhist temples and Daoist sites in the wider mountain landscape attest to the presence of other traditions.

Neo-Confucian writers disputed Buddhist views of self, attachment and withdrawal even as they addressed questions of personal cultivation that Buddhist teachers had long discussed. Later, Ming thinker Wang Yangming differed from Zhu Xi’s followers over the relation between moral knowledge and action. These disputes mattered for what teachers asked students to practice.

Some of those crossings can be traced through institutions. From the thirteenth century, Japanese Zen monks who had studied in China brought back works by Song Confucian thinkers. Those writings were read in Japanese Zen monasteries long before the Tokugawa academy at Yushima. A monastery could be a conduit for ideas that later teachers debated in a different setting.

In Joseon Korea, the state academy in Seoul prepared students for classical learning and government service. Locally supported seowon combined study with honoring earlier scholars. At Jongmyo the royal family’s rituals served a different purpose, using offerings, music and rites to affirm the dynasty’s relationship with its ancestors.

In Hanoi, the Temple of Literature and its academy developed at the Vietnamese royal capital. Later steles name successful candidates and sometimes their home villages. The inscriptions preserve evidence of who received official credentials and how the court represented scholarly achievement. In Tokugawa Japan, the Yushima Seidō shrine and school trained readers of the classics within a shogunate setting. Courts and teachers adapted shared texts to local institutions and forms of authority.

A temple hall could honor a teacher or ancestors, an academy could support reading and discussion, and a stele could preserve the names of successful candidates. Some places combined several purposes. At Qufu the Kong family residence adds evidence of the hereditary privileges and obligations that could grow around public honor for a teacher. Confucian texts, ceremonies and education therefore shaped social hierarchies as well as ideals for how people should exercise power.
The founding dates of schools and shrines mark particular institutional choices. Later reconstructions and continuing use are part of the history of each site.
